strengths: Introduces a large, well-engineered benchmark (DOMINO) with 35 tasks, 117K trajectories, 5 embodiments, and a principled three-tier dynamics taxonomy (predictable low-order, predictable high-order, stochastic/abrupt) parameterized by a scalar dynamics coefficient, enabling controlled difficulty scaling absent from prior static-world benchmarks.

Proposes a sensible and well-motivated metric suite (SR plus a continuous Manipulation Score with penalties for unsafe/erratic behavior) that goes beyond binary success, useful for future comparisons.

Extensive experimentation: systematic static-vs-dynamic comparisons across multiple VLA backbones, an informative oracle experiment isolating the role of ground-truth future trajectories, thorough ablations (history representation, prediction horizon, history length), cross-level/cross-coefficient generalization studies, and data-scaling analysis.

PUMA architecture is a reasonable, clearly described design (scene-centric historical optical flow + object-centric DINO-supervised future world queries) that adds negligible inference overhead (confirmed via latency benchmarking) while yielding consistent improvements over multiple strong baselines (π0, π0.5, OpenVLA-OFT, RDT, etc.) across dynamic interception and tracking task types.

Includes real-robot validation on a physical dual-arm platform with LoRA adaptation from simulation, showing sim-to-real transfer of the proposed dynamics-aware design, and demonstrates that dynamic training data can transfer beneficially back to static tasks, adding a useful empirical finding for the community.

Supplementary material is unusually thorough (per-task breakdowns for all 35 tasks across four transfer settings, failure-mode analysis, detailed construction pipeline for spatiotemporal synchronization, explicit limitations/future-work discussion).
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains very low even for the proposed method (17.2% SR on the main benchmark, single-digit-to-teens percentages on many individual tasks), which raises questions about whether the benchmark's difficulty/success criteria are well calibrated for meaningful method differentiation, and leaves unclear how close PUMA's gains bring the field to practically useful performance.

The synthetic data generation pipeline uses a kinematic 'stop-on-contact' simplification for object dynamics, and objects are effectively pre-scripted based on back-calculated timing; this idealizes the interception problem (e.g., no sensor noise in target velocity, no unmodeled contact physics before grasp) and may not fully capture real dynamic-manipulation challenges, a limitation the authors do acknowledge.

Real-world validation, while a plus, is limited in scope (5 tasks, 20 trials/task, only linear/Level-1-like dynamics generated via string-pulling), so it does not strongly test generalization to Level 2/3 or more naturalistic real dynamic disturbances (e.g., human-driven motion).

The technical novelty of PUMA is somewhat incremental: it combines existing building blocks (Farneback optical flow, GroundingDINO+SAM2, frozen DINO feature supervision, learnable query tokens) in a new but not conceptually deep way; the core idea of auxiliary future-feature prediction is similar in spirit to existing world-model-augmented VLA works (e.g., DreamVLA) cited by the authors, with the main claimed distinction being object-centric vs scene-centric prediction.

Some benchmark design choices (e.g., fixed α=0.1 as the primary evaluation setting throughout most experiments, task selection/criteria for success in stochastic Level-3 scenarios) are not deeply justified, and minor inconsistencies appear across tables/figures (e.g., slightly different π0.5/ACT numbers between Fig. 1 and Table 1).
